name: Hyaluronidase lip filler dissolving

lead: Hyaluronidase is the undo button for hyaluronic acid lip filler. People use it to fix lumps, migrated filler or an overfilled look and bring lips back to a shape they prefer.

The enzyme cleaves the bonds in hyaluronic acid, lowering the viscosity of the gel so the body clears the fragments. It does not act on non-hyaluronic fillers such as PMMA or fat. The clinical literature on lip use consists mainly of clinical practice and case-based reports, and Wikipedia describes it as the best treatment option for dissolving lip filler or treating related complications.

paras: A clinician injects it into the areas of filler that need reducing, and the change shows as the filler breaks down over a short period. Some people dissolve all the filler to start over, others only a lumpy or asymmetric spot before refilling. Results depend on the filler type and the practitioner.

Hyaluronidase is a prescription medicine in the United States, with several animal-derived and recombinant products approved since 2004. Reported concerns include injection-site reactions and, rarely, hypersensitivity. It only works on hyaluronic acid fillers, so people with other filler types need a different approach.

angle.text: Users and clinicians use hyaluronidase to dissolve hyaluronic acid filler and fix lumpy, uneven or unwanted lip volume. The enzyme breaks down the filler, so the change is visible as it dissolves. Evidence for this use comes mostly from clinical practice and case reports.

lead: Hyaluronidase is a family of enzymes that break down hyaluronic acid, a sugar-based polymer found naturally in connective tissue.[1] Medically it is used to help other drugs and fluids spread through tissue, for example alongside local anesthetics in eye surgery and for fluids given under the skin.[1]

In aesthetic medicine it is injected to dissolve hyaluronic acid-based dermal fillers, including those placed in the lips.[1][2] Wikipedia describes it as the best treatment option for dissolving lip filler or treating related complications.[1] It does not break down non-hyaluronic fillers, which include several synthetic and permanent materials.[2]

Hyaluronidase products have been FDA-approved in the United States since 2004.[1] Published trial evidence specifically on lip filler dissolving was not located for this article; the clinical literature on the topic consists mainly of clinical practice and case-based reports.
infobox: First US approval of a product

paras: In cosmetic dermatology, hyaluronidase is used to dissolve hyaluronic acid fillers when the result is unwanted, for example lumps, asymmetry or overcorrection.[1][2] Overfilling of the lips can give an exaggerated appearance sometimes mockingly called a trout pout.[3]

Outside aesthetics, hyaluronidase increases tissue permeability so that other drugs disperse faster. It is used with local anesthetics in ophthalmic surgery, for subcutaneous fluid administration, to aid contrast agents in urography, and in extravasation of certain solutions.[1]

Hyaluronidases lower the viscosity of hyaluronic acid and so increase the permeability of tissue.[1] Most hyaluronic acid fillers are cross-linked with BDDE to last longer in the body, which is why they persist for months rather than days.[2]

Filler procedures themselves carry risks including bruising, redness, swelling, infection, allergic reactions, lumps and, rarely, vascular occlusion with skin necrosis or vision loss.[2] Hyaluronidase is the agent clinicians reach for in such complications.[1]
Wikipedia's hyaluronidase article does not detail the enzyme's own side effects.[1]

Karl Meyer proposed a classification of hyaluronidases in 1971.[1] In the US, Vitrase (ovine) was approved in May 2004, Amphadase (bovine) in October 2004, Hydase (bovine) in October 2005 and Hylenex Recombinant, a human recombinant product, in December 2005.[1] Hyaluronidase is also now a component of subcutaneous formulations of several biologic drugs.[1]
Dermal fillers are regulated as medical devices in the US, with a provider required to inject them, whereas in the UK and EEA they are non-prescription devices that require a CE mark.[2]

In online looksmaxxing discussion, dissolving is raised by people who are unhappy with filler results, including some who report filler that migrated or persisted for years. Those accounts are individual reports and are not clinical data.
No studies found. No clinical trial of hyaluronidase for lip filler dissolving was identified. Registered trials of hyaluronidase concern other uses, such as eye surgery and nerve-block anesthesia.

timeline.event: Karl Meyer classifies hyaluronidases into three groups.[1]
